exercises.q: Mary often wears her hair in pigtails.
exercises.why: **носит** is the present tense (3rd person singular) of **носить** (to carry, to bear (a burden)) — the many-directions (or there-and-back) verb of its pair, with **нести** for one direction. present: я ношу́ · ты но́сишь · он но́сит · мы но́сим · вы но́сите · они но́сят. — Wiktionary, «носить» (CC BY-SA 4.0).  «Multidirectional verbs describe: 1. General motion, referring to ability or habitual motion, without reference to direction or destination; 2. Movement in various directions; 3. Repetition of completed trips; 4. In the past tense, a single completed round trip.» — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0).  «The verb "to carry" in Russian is rendered in two ways depending upon the way of carrying: on foot — носить-нести, понести; by vehicle — возить-везти, повезти.» — DLI, Lesson 78.  «to carry (on foot) — repeated function: носить — ношу, -сишь; носил; буду носить; actual function: нести — несу, -ёшь; нёс; буду нести; perfective: понести — понёс; понесу, -ёшь.» — DLI, Lesson 78.  «часто» marks a repeated or habitual action, which is the job of the many-directions verb.  Compare: «Он носит портфель.» (He carries a briefcase.) — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0). «Она несёт домашнее задание на занятия.» (She is taking her assignment to class.) — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0).  The other choice: **несёт** is from **нести**, the one-direction verb.  ·  Sentence and translation from Tatoeba (CC BY 2.0 FR).
exercises.context: Unprefixed verbs of motion, which are all imperfective, divide into pairs based on the direction of the movement (uni- or multidirectional — sometimes referred to as determinate/indeterminate or definite/indefinite). (Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0))

exercises.q: You know how to drive, don't you?
exercises.why: **водить** (the infinitive) (to lead, to conduct, to guide) — the many-directions (or there-and-back) verb of its pair, with **вести** for one direction. — Wiktionary, «водить» (CC BY-SA 4.0).  «Multidirectional verbs describe: 1. General motion, referring to ability or habitual motion, without reference to direction or destination; 2. Movement in various directions; 3. Repetition of completed trips; 4. In the past tense, a single completed round trip.» — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0).  «to lead, to conduct — repeated function: водить — вожу, -дишь; водил; буду водить; actual function: вести — веду, -ёшь; вёл; буду вести; perfective: повести — повёл; поведу, -ёшь.» — DLI, Lesson 78.  «This verb also follows the pattern of "going verbs". Note the following meanings: 1. to lead, to take: Я веду моего сына в школу. Я каждый день вожу его в школу. 2. to drive: Кто ведёт эту машину? Он не умеет водить машину. 3. to conduct: Противник ведёт огонь. 4. to behave oneself: Этот мальчик плохо ведёт себя. Note that in the last two examples (3 and 4) only the actual function verb "вести" can be used. (Never "водить").» — DLI, Lesson 78.  «умеешь» speaks of ability or liking — general motion, again the many-directions verb.  Compare: «Она водила свою подругу в театр.» (She took her friend to the theatre.) — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0). «Она умеет водить машину.» (She knows how to drive a car.) — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0).  The other choice: **вести** is from **вести**, the one-direction verb.  ·  Sentence and translation from Tatoeba (CC BY 2.0 FR).

In the past tense, a single completed round trip.» — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0).  «The verb "to carry" in Russian is rendered in two ways depending upon the way of carrying: on foot — носить-нести, понести; by vehicle — возить-везти, повезти.» — DLI, Lesson 78.  «to carry (on foot) — repeated function: носить — ношу, -сишь; носил; буду носить; actual function: нести — несу, -ёшь; нёс; буду нести; perfective: понести — понёс; понесу, -ёшь.» — DLI, Lesson 78.  «всегда» marks a repeated or habitual action, which is the job of the many-directions verb.  Compare: «Он носит портфель.» (He carries a briefcase.) — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0). «Она несёт домашнее задание на занятия.» (She is taking her assignment to class.) — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0).  The other choice: **несёшь** is from **нести**, the one-direction verb.  ·  Sentence and translation from Tatoeba (CC BY 2.0 FR).

exercises.q: Honey badgers are usually nocturnal.
exercises.why: **ведут** is the present tense (3rd person plural) of **вести** (to lead, to preside over, to chair) — the one-direction verb of its pair, with **водить** for many directions. present: я веду́ · ты ведёшь · он ведёт · мы ведём · вы ведёте · они веду́т. — Wiktionary, «вести» (CC BY-SA 4.0).  «Unidirectional verbs describe motion in progress in one direction.» — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0).  «to lead, to conduct — repeated function: водить — вожу, -дишь; водил; буду водить; actual function: вести — веду, -ёшь; вёл; буду вести; perfective: повести — повёл; поведу, -ёшь.» — DLI, Lesson 78.  «This verb also follows the pattern of "going verbs". Note the following meanings: 1. to lead, to take: Я веду моего сына в школу. Я каждый день вожу его в школу. 2. to drive: Кто ведёт эту машину? Он не умеет водить машину. 3. to conduct: Противник ведёт огонь. 4. to behave oneself: Этот мальчик плохо ведёт себя. Note that in the last two examples (3 and 4) only the actual function verb "вести" can be used. (Never "водить").» — DLI, Lesson 78.  Compare: «Учитель вёл школьников на экскурсию.» (The teacher was taking the children to a field trip.) — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0). «Она водила свою подругу в театр.» (She took her friend to the theatre.) — Wikipedia, «Russian grammar» § Verbs of motion (CC BY-SA 4.0).  The other choice: **водят** is from **водить**, the many-directions verb.  ·  Sentence and translation from Tatoeba (CC BY 2.0 FR).
